summary: This memo describes the Internet Gopher protocol, a distributed document search and retrieval system built around menus, along with an overview of how to implement clients and servers. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Gopher was an early way of browsing the Internet using simple menus you could pick from, a bit like the web before the web took over.

questions: how does a gopher menu work
subtitle: A menu-driven way to browse and fetch documents from many servers, built to be simple enough for 1 MB desktop machines.

tldr.problem: Universities wanted departments to publish documents from inexpensive desktop machines and let users browse them across many servers, without heavy software on slow computers.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection, sends one line of text called a selector, and the server replies with a menu or document ending in a period on a line by itself, then closes the connection. Each menu line carries an item type, a display name, a selector, a host and a port.
tldr.outcome: The protocol keeps the server stateless and pushes new features into new item types, so clients can grow by recognizing a new type character. This memo is Informational and does not specify an Internet standard.

facts.label: End of a text reply
facts.value: A period on a line by itself

today: RFC 1436 is an Informational memo, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes Gopher as it stood in March 1993, adapted from the document first issued by the University of Minnesota's Microcomputer Center in 1991.

sections.title: Why Model It on a File System
sections.content:
The Internet Gopher protocol is a distributed document search and retrieval system. Documents live on many autonomous servers, but client software shows the user one hierarchy of items and directories that looks like a file system. The memo gives four reasons: hierarchies are familiar, they can be expressed in a simple syntax, they suit departments publishing from inexpensive desktop machines, and a file system metaphor can be extended with item types.

The simple syntax was chosen so that it is easy to debug. The memo notes that you can use Telnet to simulate a Gopher client's requests and read the server's responses, with no special tools.
sections.eli5: Everyone already knows folders and files, so Gopher shows the whole Internet as folders and files. That way nobody has to learn anything new.

sections.title: How a Gopher Exchange Works
sections.content:
A client connects over TCP to a server, which should listen on port 70, and sends a selector: a line of text that may be empty. The server answers with a block of text terminated by a period on a line by itself and closes the connection. No state is retained by the server between transactions. The memo says this simplicity comes from the need to build servers and clients quickly for slow, small desktop computers such as 1 MB Macs and DOS machines.

An empty selector means list what you have. The reply is a menu, one item per line, and each line ends with CR LF. The client keeps only one piece of configuration: the name and port of a well-known server.

To follow a menu item, the client opens a new connection to the host and port named in that line and sends the item's selector. The user sees only the display name. The selector is opaque, so the client must never modify it.
sections.eli5: You tell the helper a word, the helper gives you a list or a page, and then hangs up. Next time you call, the helper has forgotten you, which keeps things simple.

sections.title: Menu Lines and Item Types
sections.content:
Each menu line has the item type as its first character, then a user display string, then a TAB, a selector, a TAB, a host name, a TAB and a port. A basic client ignores any extra tab-delimited fields. The display string should be kept under 70 characters and the selector no longer than 255 characters.

The base types are 0 (file), 1 (directory) and 7 (search). Others cover a CSO phone-book server (2), an error (3), BinHexed Macintosh and uuencoded files (4, 6), binary files (5, 9), a text telnet session (8), a tn3270 session (T), GIF graphics (g) and other images (I). Types 5 and 9 have no closing period: the client must read until the TCP connection closes. A + entry marks a redundant copy of the server in the preceding entry.

Characters 0 through Z are reserved, and local experiments should use other characters. A client that does not understand a type may simply ignore the item or show it as an unknown type. In text files, lines that begin with a period get an extra period so the document is not cut short, and the client strips it.
sections.eli5: The first letter of each line is like a little sticker that says what kind of thing it is: a folder, a note, a picture, or a search box.

sections.title: Servers, Search and Gateways
sections.content:
Gopher links form an arbitrary graph, not necessarily a tree. An institution is expected to have one well-known top-level server, possibly duplicated to avoid a single point of failure. Departments register their servers with it, but they may also link to any server they like. The memo recommends giving registered servers DNS alias names (CNAME) so a service can move without reconfiguring clients.

A search server (type 7) takes the selector, a tab and the search words, and returns what looks like a directory listing of matching documents. Spaces between words are usually an implied AND. Full-text indexes can be split over several index servers and searched in parallel without the client knowing. Other services can be reached through gateway servers, such as Gopher-to-FTP, Gopher-to-archie and Gopher-to-WAIS, which means clients do not have to be modified to use a new resource.

The CSO type exists for historical reasons: the University of Minnesota's phone-book servers already used the CSO protocol, so it seemed simplest to engulf them.
sections.eli5: Any shelf can point to any other shelf, even one in a different building. A special search desk can look through lots of pages and give you a list of the ones that mention your words.

sections.title: Building Clients and Servers
sections.content:
A client sends the retrieval string and shows the result. It may keep a stack of visited locations so the user can back out, show several windows, or cache whole directories to avoid network transactions. Smart clients can pick randomly between cloned primary servers to balance load and move to the other if one seems down. A DNS answer that rotates addresses can do the same job.

On the server side, the retrieval string might be a file path, the name of a script, or a query that generates the result. The server reads up to a CR LF or a TAB, whichever comes first. The memo states a philosophy: intelligence is held by the server, the protocol stays minimal, servers should send plain text unless a file must be raw binary, and clients should do something reasonable with odd characters.
sections.eli5: The clever work happens at the helper's desk, not in the phone line. Your own program just asks politely and shows whatever comes back.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The memo's Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed. Gopher as described has no authentication, and the only login information it mentions is the user name placed in the selector for type 8 and T telnet sessions.
sections.eli5: The rulebook does not say anything about keeping secrets, so it does not promise any.
